stemMd: In the last paragraph the narrator looks at the tide clock and finds "that I already knew what they would say." This statement most strongly suggests that the narrator has:

options.label: A
options.textMd: concluded that the tide clock and the kitchen stove clock measure the same thing after all.

options.label: B
options.textMd: discovered that the clock had been broken all along and had to be reset.

options.label: C
options.textMd: memorised the departure times Nan used for the crossing at Ardvane.

options.label: D
options.textMd: learned to read the state of the tide directly, so that the clock now only confirms what the narrator can work out from the water.

explanationMd:
Track what changes across the passage. At the start, the narrator can see the water but says plainly, "I could see the water; I could not see the hour in it" — the clock is unreadable because the tide itself is unreadable. The turning point is the August evening: after watching the flats for an hour and a half, the narrator finally sees slack water and hears Nan name it.

Only then does the narrator go inside and find the clock's two hands already intelligible. Nothing about the clock has changed; what has changed is the narrator's ability to read the tide. That is exactly what choice B says.

To check the answer, ask what the sentence would have to mean for each of the other choices to be true — a memorised timetable, a repair, or a claim that the two clocks agree — and look for a line in the passage that supports it. There is none: the passage says the schedule was never printed and changed every day, never says the clock was repaired, and states that the tide clock "never agreed with the clock on the stove."

distractorRationale.c: Assumes there were fixed departure times to memorise. The second paragraph says the opposite: the schedule was never printed "because it changed every day," and Nan twice refused the bus company's request for fixed times.
distractorRationale.b: Takes the child's early belief that the clock was "broken" as the passage's actual position. That belief is presented as a misunderstanding the narrator held "for the first eleven summers," and nothing in the passage describes a repair or a reset.
distractorRationale.a: Contradicts the first paragraph, which states that the tide clock "never agreed with the clock on the stove." The point of the ending is that the narrator can now read a different measure, not that the two clocks turned out to be equivalent.

accessibilityText: The question asks what the narrator means by the final sentence of the passage, in which the narrator looks at the two hands of the numberless tide clock and finds that the narrator already knew what they would say.

independentSolve.workingNotes: Paragraph 4-5 show the narrator watching the flats and independently identifying the moment of slack water; the final line then says the clock's hands only told what was already known, so the narrator can now read the tide from the water itself. A fails because paragraph 2 says the schedule changed daily and was never printed, so there are no departure times to memorise; C reverses the arc (the eleven-year-old's belief that the clock was broken is what the narrator outgrows); D is unsupported and contradicts the stove-clock/tide-clock contrast.

review.notes: Author solved the item and then tried to defend each distractor in turn. A fails on "a schedule that nobody printed because it changed every day"; C mistakes the narrator's childhood misreading for fact; D is contradicted by "never agreed with the clock on the stove." Awaiting an independent blind solve before any change of state. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
